title: Neither do I condemn thee (John 8:1–11)
hook: the crowd has stones, he writes in the dust, and they leave one by one

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man up a tree, and the line today salvation came to this house. Did someone surprise you? Day fifty-five.

Early morning in the Temple courts. Jesus is sitting down, teaching a crowd. Suddenly there's a commotion. Some scribes and Pharisees push through, dragging a woman, and stand her in the middle of everyone. She's been caught, they say, in the act of adultery. The Law of Moses says such a woman should be stoned. So what do you say? John tells us plainly that it's a trap. If he says let her go, he's set aside the Law. If he says stone her, where's the mercy he's known for? Everyone waits. There are stones within reach. And Jesus doesn't answer. He bends down and starts writing on the ground with his finger. Today: the dust, the stones, and the woman in the middle.
screen: `A WOMAN DRAGGED INTO THE CROWD.` → `A TRAP.` → `HE WRITES IN THE DUST.`

segments.voice: What did he write? The Gospel never says. People have guessed for centuries: Saint Jerome and others imagined he wrote the accusers' own sins in the dirt. But John leaves it blank, and it's honest to leave it blank too. They keep pressing him. So he straightens up and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." Then he bends down and writes again. He doesn't stare them down. He gives them room. And one by one they go away, John says, beginning with the eldest. The oldest ones leave first. Maybe they had the most to remember. Until it's just Jesus, and the woman, still standing there. And here's something worth noticing: where is the man? You can't be caught in adultery alone. The text is silent. Then Jesus looks up and speaks to her, maybe the first person all morning to speak to her rather than about her. Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you? No one, Lord. And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Neither will I condemn thee. Go, and now sin no more." Both halves matter. No condemnation. And a new life. He doesn't pretend nothing happened, and he doesn't throw a stone. One more thing a scholar would tell you: this passage is missing from the oldest Greek manuscripts of John, and in some later ones it turns up in a different place. The Catholic Church receives it as sacred Scripture, part of the Gospel, and it's read at Mass in Lent.
screen: `WHAT DID HE WRITE? JOHN DOESN'T SAY.` · `LET HIM WITHOUT SIN CAST FIRST.` · `ONE BY ONE, THE ELDEST FIRST.` · `NO CONDEMNING, AND A NEW LIFE.` · then, large: `GO, AND NOW SIN NO MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put down one judgment. Settle and breathe. Think of a person you've been holding a stone for. Someone whose mistake you keep replaying, maybe someone the whole group is talking about. Picture the stone in your hand. Feel its weight. You don't have to decide that what they did was fine. Just open your hand, and set it down in the dust. Then, if you want, turn the same mercy toward yourself. If you pray, you can hear his words spoken to you. The bell holds the time.
Neither do I condemn thee. A woman in the middle of a crowd with stones, and the only one without sin sets her free. Today's word.
screen: `NEITHER DO I CONDEMN THEE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: go, and sin no more. Today, put down one stone, and walk one step into something new. Day fifty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics hear this Gospel on the Fifth Sunday of Lent in Year C, and it is often preached before confession as a picture of mercy that frees a person and sends them into a new life.

original.note: Greek: to condemn, to judge against. The word Jesus uses to the woman: neither do I condemn you.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus says it's fine.
what it means: no condemnation, and a new life. he doesn't throw a stone, and he doesn't pretend nothing happened.
what a scholar hears: the passage is missing from the oldest Greek manuscripts of John and wanders in later ones; the Church receives it as Scripture.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of John 8:7 and 8:11 given from memory; confirm. The Douay-Rheims reads 'Neither will I condemn thee' and 'Go, and now sin no more'; the index title and carry follow the KJV ('Neither do I condemn thee', 'go, and sin no more'). The script keeps the index wording as required; a Keeper may prefer the Douay-Rheims forms in the index.

Manuscript note: the pericope (John 7:53–8:11) is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts (e.g. P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) and appears elsewhere in some (after John 7:36, 21:25, or Luke 21:38). Catholic teaching receives it as canonical. Confirm phrasing.
Jerome's suggestion that he wrote the accusers' sins: attributed to Jerome (Against the Pelagians 2.17); confirm, or change to 'some early writers'.
Read on the Fifth Sunday of Lent, Year C: confirm.
The Law cited (Leviticus 20:10, Deuteronomy 22:22) prescribes death for both man and woman; the script notes only that the man is absent.
